    Cotton, wool and the day labourers

    One morning, one riverbank, the whole circuit of capital: who paid, who sold, who worked, and what was left.

    What you will see with your own eyes

    You start at Kita-Senju, the first post town on the old Nikkō road. You walk south down that road and cross the Sumida on Senju Ōhashi, a steel bridge of 1927.

    On the far bank you reach Minami-Senju 6-chōme. Here stood Japan's first modern woollen mill, opened by the state in 1879. A stretch of its brick wall, built in 1911 to 1914 after the 1910 flood, survives. Two panels reportedly stand in a supermarket's bicycle park. A factory wall now guards bicycles. You may enjoy that.

    A few minutes on is Kotsukappara, Edo's execution ground from 1651. The "beheading Jizō" of 1741 still sits there. In 1771 doctors watched a dissection here, and it led to Japan's first Western anatomy text.

    Then you follow the river east and cross Shirahige Bridge into Sumida. In front of you rises a housing estate with no known equal in Japan for length. Eighteen blocks, 40 metres high, run in one line for 1.2 kilometres. The line is a fire wall. Look for the fire shutters on the balconies, the water cannons on the fifth floor and the tanks on the roof. Behind it lies a park built to shelter about 80,000 people. This wall stands on the land of the Kanebō cotton mill. In Kanebō Park, a stone marks the birthplace of Kanegafuchi Spinning.

    You walk back west to Namidabashi, "the bridge of tears", and into San'ya, Tokyo's day-labour district. You pass the Jōhoku Labour and Welfare Centre, Tamahime Park and the shopping street that lost its arcade roof in 2018. You drink coffee at Café Bach, roasting here since 1968. Lunch is soba at Tōjimaya, a house founded in 1887. That is the same year Kanebō was founded across the river.

    Why it means something

    The wool mill was Japan's state answer to an import bill. The army's uniforms were largely bought abroad, and that drained foreign currency. So the government built a mill. Its first director, Inoue Shōzō, had learned wool-making in Germany. From 1888 the Army Ministry ran it and expanded it. After defeat in 1945 production stopped. A private wool firm bought it and closed it in 1960. A baseball stadium took the land from 1962 to 1972; a sports centre holds it now.

    Kanebō is the private half of the story. It began in 1887 as the Tokyo Cotton Merchants' Company, at Kanegafuchi. Its mill was finished in 1889. Mitsui Bank became its main bank. In 1894 the bank sent a young man named Mutō Sanji into the firm. He rose to run it, and became president in 1921. Under him Kanebō ranked first in Japan by sales. Mutō called good treatment of workers "the best investment". In 1902 he set up a nursery and a girls' school inside the mill he ran. The firm also founded a mutual aid society. That was paternalism as a management system, sold as family.

    The ending is pure irony. The Tokyo spinning plant became a cosmetics factory in 1963 and closed in 1969. Tokyo bought the land. Planners feared a firestorm in the dense wooden streets that grew up after the 1923 earthquake. So they turned a cotton mill into a fortress against fire, built from 1975 to 1982. The small workshops it displaced were moved into one shared factory building at the west end.

    San'ya supplied the hands. In Edo it was cheap inns on the highway. In Meiji it housed rickshaw men. Before the war it already held day labourers. After 1945 tents for bombed-out families became flophouses. In 1961 about 20,000 workers lived in about 300 of them. They built Olympic Tokyo. Riots recurred through the 1960s, and in 1966 the name San'ya was taken off the address map. A 2021 survey counted about 3,000 residents, nine in ten on welfare. Many flophouses now take backpackers.

    What it gives your six volumes

    This is Volume 1 in another country. You can stand on a cotton mill site and ask the six questions of it directly.

    Where the capital came from. Two answers sit a river apart. The wool mill was state money, spent to stop a currency drain. Kanebō began as a cotton merchants' company, and Mitsui Bank later stood behind it. You will see both sites before ten o'clock.

    Where the machines and know-how came from. A director who learned wool-making in Germany. Japan carried the know-how home in one man's training, much as Slater carried it in his memory. You can test that thought on the spot.

    Where the workers came from. San'ya is your answer, as a place. It shows the reserve of labour that the factory age needed, and what became of it once the work moved on.

    How work was organised and disciplined. Mutō's nursery, school and mutual aid society belong beside your Lowell bell and Sunday school. The brick wall itself is a lesson in enclosure.

    Who bought the product. For the wool mill, the buyer was the army. That is a market made by the state, and it will serve you again in later volumes.

    What happened to the surplus, and to the land. Kanebō grew into Japan's largest firm by sales. Its founding ground ended as public housing and a fire wall. Few places show the end of a wave so plainly.

    The walk also touches Volume 3. The 1927 steel bridge is on your route. A 45-minute add-on reaches the monument to the Senju coal power station, which ran from 1926 to 1964. Its four chimneys were famous across the city. San'ya's Olympic builders belong to the high-growth years of Volume 4.

    What you will understand at 12:30

    At 07:00 the circuit of capital is a diagram in your notes. By 12:30 it has a map. You will have walked from the money to the mill, to the workers' district and back. You will see that the state and a bank both started factories here, for different buyers. You will see that the labour pool outlived the mills it served. And you will have seen what a city does with a dead mill: it builds a wall against the next disaster. "For better and worse" will stop being a refrain and become a street.

    What it asks of you

    It asks for legs. This is about 9 kilometres, mostly on foot and calm away from the main roads. You can save 1 kilometre by taking the train to Minami-Senju. Money is light: about ¥2,100 for trains, coffee and lunch. The exact spot of the wool mill wall is not confirmed, so allow a few minutes to find it. The ward history museum on the same block opens at 09:30, after you pass.

    It also asks for manners. San'ya is people's home, not a sight. Take no photos of people, queues or hotel doorways. Do not linger outside the welfare centre. Walk through Tamahime Park without a camera. At Shirahige-higashi, keep to public paths and never photograph into windows or balconies. Buy your coffee and your lunch locally. That is the fair exchange, and it is also a very good lunch.
